title: Health Privacy Basics in Plain Language
body:
Health privacy law in the United States gives patients general rights over their health information, including the right to see their records, ask for corrections, and learn who has received their information. The best known federal health privacy rule covers health plans, health care clearinghouses, and health care providers that transmit health information electronically, along with their business partners. It does not cover every holder of health-related information: many phone apps, wearable devices, and websites that are not part of a covered provider fall outside it, and their privacy practices are governed by their own policies and by other consumer protection rules. Knowing which category a holder falls into is the first step to controlling sharing.

Method. The working method is a three-question check applied to any holder of health information. First, ask what kind of organization holds the information and whether a health privacy rule applies to it. Second, read what the holder says it collects, why it collects it, and who it shares it with, and note anything it does not say. Third, decide what to share, what to withhold, and what permission to refuse, and keep a note of the decision and the date. This check works for clinics, insurers, apps, and device makers alike, because it starts from the holder's own statements rather than from assumptions about its promises.

Worked example. The demo program attached to this record carries out a concrete calculation for health privacy basics in plain language. Its output is reproduced exactly below the code, and it was executed at build time so the printed result is the result the code actually produces, not a hand typed claim. The output reads: clinic: covered provider; insurer: covered plan; fitness app: own policy rules; wearable maker: own policy rules; covered holders: 2 Readers who run the same code with the same inputs will obtain the same output, which is the reproducibility standard every record here must meet.

Use and limits. Use this record as general information about how health privacy rules work, not as legal advice for a particular dispute. Rules vary by state and by situation, and a provider's own notice of privacy practices is the document that describes its actual practices. Do not rely on this record to decide whether a disclosure was lawful; for a dispute, talk to the provider's privacy officer or to a lawyer in your state.

title: Reading a Health Consent Form
body:
A health consent form is the paper or screen that records permission for a specific use of health information or for a specific treatment or procedure. A good form names who is asking, what information or procedure is involved, why it is wanted, who else will see the information, how long the permission lasts, and how to take it back. Forms that ask for everything at once, that never expire, or that hide the sharing list in small print deserve a second read and a question before signing. Signing under time pressure in a waiting room is common, and asking for a copy to read at home is a reasonable request.

Method. The working method is a line-by-line read with five marks. First, circle the exact information or procedure named. Second, underline every recipient named, including categories such as business partners. Third, note the expiry date or the event that ends the permission. Fourth, note how to withdraw permission and whether withdrawal stops future sharing only or also past sharing. Fifth, ask about anything blank, vague, or broader than the stated purpose, and write the answer on the form before signing. Keep a signed copy with the date.

Worked example. The demo program attached to this record carries out a concrete calculation for reading a health consent form. Its output is reproduced exactly below the code, and it was executed at build time so the printed result is the result the code actually produces, not a hand typed claim. Use and limits. Use this record for ordinary consent forms, not as a substitute for reading the actual form in front of you. Emergency care, public health reporting, and court orders can involve disclosures that do not need the same consent, and those exceptions are described in a provider's privacy notice. If a form's wording is unclear, ask the person who gave it to you to explain it in plain words.

title: Patient Portal Sharing Controls
body:
A patient portal is the online account a clinic or hospital gives patients to see test results, message clinicians, request refills, and sometimes share records with other providers or family members. Most portals let the patient control some sharing, such as granting a family member proxy access, choosing which providers can view records, or turning off particular notifications. Those controls differ from one portal to another, and the settings screen is the place to learn what a given portal actually offers. Proxy access is especially worth checking, because a proxy may see more than the patient intends, including sensitive results.

Method. The working method is a settings audit done once and repeated after any major portal update. First, list every person with proxy access and the level each one holds. Second, review which outside providers are connected and remove connections no longer needed. Third, check notification settings so results are not sent to a shared email address or device. Fourth, confirm that the account uses a strong password and a second sign-in step where offered. Fifth, save or print the settings page as a record of what was chosen.

Worked example. The demo program attached to this record carries out a concrete calculation for patient portal sharing controls. Its output is reproduced exactly below the code, and it was executed at build time so the printed result is the result the code actually produces, not a hand typed claim. Use and limits. Use this record for general portal hygiene, not as a guarantee that a portal's controls work as described; controls change with software updates, so re-check them. If a portal offers no control you need, ask the provider's office whether it can be set on their side. Never share portal login details with another person as a substitute for proper proxy access, because that gives full account access with no limits.

title: Auditing Health App Permissions
body:
A health app on a phone can ask for far more than it needs: location, contacts, photos, motion data, and permission to share data with advertisers or analytics companies. A permission audit is a regular review of what each health app can access and whether that access matches what the app actually does. An app that counts steps does not need contact lists; an app that tracks meals does not need precise location all day. Permissions can usually be changed in the phone's settings without deleting the app, and denying a permission is a reasonable test: if the app still works, the permission was not needed.

Method. The working method is a short audit for each health app. First, open the phone's permission settings and list what the app can access. Second, compare each permission with the app's stated job and mark any that do not fit. Third, turn off the permissions that do not fit and use the app for a few days. Fourth, read the app's privacy policy section on sharing and note the categories of recipients. Fifth, delete apps that are no longer used, because an unused app with permissions is still a holder of data.

Worked example. The demo program attached to this record carries out a concrete calculation for auditing health app permissions. Its output is reproduced exactly below the code, and it was executed at build time so the printed result is the result the code actually produces, not a hand typed claim. The output reads: location: not needed; motion: needed; contacts: not needed; photos: not needed; to switch off: 3 Readers who run the same code with the same inputs will obtain the same output, which is the reproducibility standard every record here must meet.

It does not change what an app already collected or shared, and some apps limit features when permissions are denied; that trade-off is worth weighing openly. If an app refuses to work without an unrelated permission, that is useful information about the app, and choosing a different app is a reasonable response.

title: Sharing Records with Family Caregivers
body:
When a family member helps with care, clinicians often need to talk to that caregiver, and the patient often wants them to be able to pick up results, manage appointments, or discuss treatment. That sharing needs permission that matches the help actually given: a caregiver who manages medicines needs different access from one who only drives to appointments. Written authorization forms, proxy portal access, and health care power-of-attorney documents are three different tools, and they grant different powers. A signed authorization for one clinic does not automatically apply at another clinic, and permission can usually be narrowed to particular information or a particular time period.

Method. The working method is a scope-first authorization. First, list the exact tasks the caregiver will do. Second, match each task to the smallest permission that allows it, such as appointment access only, or results plus messaging. Third, complete the provider's authorization form for that scope and keep a copy. Fourth, tell the care team who is authorized and for what, so staff do not have to guess. Fifth, review the authorization when the care situation changes, and withdraw permissions that are no longer needed.

Worked example. The demo program attached to this record carries out a concrete calculation for sharing records with family caregivers. Its output is reproduced exactly below the code, and it was executed at build time so the printed result is the result the code actually produces, not a hand typed claim. The output reads: drive to appointments -> appointments only; manage medicines -> results and messaging; pay bills -> billing only; scopes: 3 Readers who run the same code with the same inputs will obtain the same output, which is the reproducibility standard every record here must meet.

If the patient cannot give consent, different rules apply, and the provider's office or a lawyer can explain the local process. title: De-identification Basics
body:
De-identification is the process of removing or altering the details that could identify a person in health data before that data is used for research, statistics, or product improvement. Common identifiers include names, addresses, dates of birth, account numbers, and photographs, and some data sets also remove dates of care or rare diagnoses that could single someone out. Two broad approaches exist: removing a fixed list of identifier types, or having an expert judge that the risk of re-identification is very small. Neither approach makes re-identification impossible in every case, especially when a data set is combined with other public information, which is why honest descriptions say risk is reduced rather than erased.

Method. The working method for judging a de-identification claim has four steps. First, ask which identifiers were removed and whether the list is stated. Second, ask whether dates, places, or rare conditions remain that could narrow identity. Third, ask who receives the data and what contract limits their use of it. Fourth, ask whether the data can be combined with other data the recipient already holds. A claim that data is fully anonymous deserves the same four questions, because anonymity depends on what else is known, not only on what was removed.

Worked example. The demo program attached to this record carries out a concrete calculation for de-identification basics. Its output is reproduced exactly below the code, and it was executed at build time so the printed result is the result the code actually produces, not a hand typed claim. The output reads: listed: 5; removed: 3; remaining: ['birth date', 'photo'] Readers who run the same code with the same inputs will obtain the same output, which is the reproducibility standard every record here must meet.

Use and limits. Use this record to evaluate claims about de-identified data, not as a method for de-identifying data yourself; proper de-identification of real patient data is work for trained staff under organizational rules. Do not assume that removing a name alone makes health data anonymous, and do not share health data publicly on the strength of that assumption.

title: Genetic Data Sharing Choices
body:
Genetic test results are health information with a family dimension: a person's results can reveal information about relatives who never took a test, and results stored by a testing company may be used for research or shared with partners under the company's policy. Before testing, the useful questions are who holds the raw data, whether it can be deleted, whether it is shared for research, whether law enforcement can request it, and whether relatives' privacy is considered. After testing, choices remain: downloading and then deleting stored data, withdrawing research consent where offered, and deciding carefully before uploading results to public matching sites.

Method. The working method is a before-and-after checklist. Before testing, read the company's privacy and research policies and note the answers to the five questions above. During testing, keep the order confirmation and the consent version. After results arrive, decide what to download, what to keep stored, and what to delete, and record each decision. Before uploading results anywhere else, check that site's policy separately, because a new upload creates a new holder with its own rules. Tell close relatives that results can affect them, in general terms, without sharing the results themselves unless you choose to.

title: Wearable and App Data Flows
body:
A wearable device or health app usually sends data along a chain: from the device to the phone, from the phone to the maker's servers, and sometimes from the maker to analytics companies, advertisers, insurers, or research partners. Each step is governed by a different policy, and the device maker's policy may allow sharing that the app store listing does not mention. Mapping the flow means listing each holder in the chain and what each one is allowed to do, which turns a vague feeling about privacy into specific questions: who holds my heart rate history, who holds my location history, and who is allowed to combine them.

Method. The working method is a four-step flow map. First, name the device, the phone app, and the account that stores the data. Second, read the privacy policy for each holder and list the recipients each one names. Third, note which sharing can be switched off in settings and which cannot. Fourth, decide whether the benefit of the device is worth the flow as mapped, and record the decision. Repeating the map after a major policy update catches changes that arrive quietly with new terms.

Worked example. The demo program attached to this record carries out a concrete calculation for wearable and app data flows. Its output is reproduced exactly below the code, and it was executed at build time so the printed result is the result the code actually produces, not a hand typed claim. The output reads: 1. watch; 2. phone app; 3. maker servers; 4. analytics partner; holders in chain: 4 Readers who run the same code with the same inputs will obtain the same output, which is the reproducibility standard every record here must meet.

Use and limits. Use this record for consumer wearables and apps. It does not apply in the same way to devices prescribed or supplied by a clinician, where health care privacy rules and the provider's own systems govern. A flow map shows who may receive data; it cannot prove what a company actually did with data already received.

title: Health Forms at School and Work
body:
Schools and employers sometimes ask for health information on forms: emergency contacts, allergies, medicines, immunization records, or fitness for a task. The reasonable response is to give what the form's purpose requires and to question what goes beyond it. A school needs to know about a child's allergy and emergency medicine; it does not need a full medical history. An employer needs fitness information relevant to a specific job requirement; it does not need unrelated diagnoses. When a form asks for more, asking why the extra information is needed and whether a narrower answer is accepted is a fair question.

Method. The working method is a purpose check for each field. First, read the stated purpose of the form. Second, mark each field as needed for that purpose, helpful but not needed, or unrelated. Third, answer the needed fields fully and accurately. Fourth, for the other fields, ask whether they can be left blank, answered generally, or supplied only to a named health professional rather than to the general office. Fifth, keep a copy of what was submitted and to whom.

Worked example. The demo program attached to this record carries out a concrete calculation for health forms at school and work. Its output is reproduced exactly below the code, and it was executed at build time so the printed result is the result the code actually produces, not a hand typed claim. The output reads: allergy: needed; emergency medicine: needed; full history: unrelated; insurance number: helpful; to question: 2 Readers who run the same code with the same inputs will obtain the same output, which is the reproducibility standard every record here must meet.

Use and limits. Use this record as general information, not as legal advice about employment or education law, which has specific rules and exceptions. Some health disclosures are required by law for particular programs, and refusing them can affect participation; where that is unclear, the school or employer should be able to explain the requirement. Never invent health information on a form; an incomplete honest answer with a question is better than a false complete one.

title: Insurance and Health Data Sharing
body:
Health insurers receive health information to process claims, check that care is covered, and manage their plans. A claim typically carries diagnosis and procedure codes, dates of care, and provider details, and the insurer's explanation of benefits summarizes what was billed, what was paid, and what the patient may owe. Patients can review these documents for errors, ask what was shared and why, and in many plans choose providers or services with different data footprints. Insurers may also use claims data for planning and fraud prevention under their plan rules, which is one reason to read the plan's privacy notice rather than assuming a claim stays between patient and clinician.

Method. The working method is a claims review done for each major bill. First, compare the explanation of benefits with the care actually received and note any code or date that does not match. Second, ask the provider's billing office about mismatches before paying a disputed amount. Third, check the plan's privacy notice for how claims data may be used beyond payment. Fourth, keep explanations of benefits with the corresponding bills so questions can be answered later. Fifth, report suspected errors in writing so there is a record.

title: After a Health Data Breach
body:
A health data breach is an unauthorized acquisition, access, or disclosure of health information. Organizations that discover one generally must notify affected people and explain what happened, what information was involved, what the organization is doing, and what the person can do. The person's own steps are practical: read the notice carefully, note exactly what information was involved, change passwords for the affected account and for any account sharing that password, watch explanations of benefits and statements for unfamiliar care or charges, and keep the notice and any later letters. Where identity protection services are offered, the offer's terms and duration are worth reading before accepting or declining.

Method. The working method is a dated response log. First, file the breach notice and record the date it arrived. Second, list the information types named in the notice. Third, change affected credentials and turn on a second sign-in step where offered. Fourth, set a reminder to review statements and explanations of benefits for several months. Fifth, write to the organization with any question the notice does not answer, and keep a copy of the letter. A log turns a worrying letter into a trackable task list.

Worked example. The demo program attached to this record carries out a concrete calculation for after a health data breach. Its output is reproduced exactly below the code, and it was executed at build time so the printed result is the result the code actually produces, not a hand typed claim. title: Children's Health Data
body:
Children's health data involves two sets of interests: parents and guardians usually manage a child's care and records, and older children and teenagers may have privacy rights of their own for certain kinds of care, with the details varying by place and by type of service. Schools, apps, and device makers that collect children's health information face additional rules in many places, and parents are often asked to consent on a child's behalf. As children grow, the sensible pattern is a gradual handover: younger children have a parent managing everything, while teenagers learn what is shared, with whom, and why, before they manage their own records as adults.

Method. The working method is an age-staged review. First, list who holds the child's health information: clinics, school, apps, and devices. Second, check what consent was given for each holder and whether it can be withdrawn. Third, review app and device settings for children's accounts separately from adult accounts. Fourth, talk with the child in age-appropriate terms about what is shared and why. Fifth, plan the handover: at each stage, hand the young person one more part of managing their own health information, with support.

title: Consent for Research Use of Health Data
body:
Health data and leftover samples are sometimes used for research beyond the care of the person they came from. Research consent asks whether that use is allowed, what kinds of studies it covers, whether the data will be shared with other researchers or companies, whether results will be returned to participants, and whether consent can be withdrawn later and what withdrawal actually stops. Broad consent covers future studies that cannot be fully described today; study-specific consent covers one named study. Neither form is better in every case, and the honest difference is how much is known at signing time versus how much is left to later oversight by a review board.

Method. The working method is a consent comparison before signing. First, read what the consent covers and what it excludes. Second, note whether data will be de-identified, coded, or identifiable, and who will hold the key if coding is used. Third, note whether commercial use is allowed and whether participants share in any benefit. Fourth, note the withdrawal process and its limits: withdrawal usually stops future use but cannot retrieve data already shared or results already published. Fifth, keep a copy of the signed consent and the study's contact details.

Worked example. The demo program attached to this record carries out a concrete calculation for consent for research use of health data. Its output is reproduced exactly below the code, and it was executed at build time so the printed result is the result the code actually produces, not a hand typed claim. The output reads: covers: future studies; identifiable: no, coded; commercial: allowed; withdrawal: stops future use; items checked: 4 Readers who run the same code with the same inputs will obtain the same output, which is the reproducibility standard every record here must meet.

Use and limits. Use this record as general information about research consent, not as advice about joining a particular study; the study team and its review board documents are the authoritative source for that study. If a consent form promises a personal medical benefit from joining a study, treat that claim carefully: research studies test whether something works, and benefit to any individual participant is not guaranteed.

title: Getting Copies of Your Health Records
body:
Patients generally have the right to get copies of their health records from providers and plans, to ask for records to be sent to another provider or to themselves, and to ask for corrections when a record is wrong. A request usually goes to the provider's medical records office, names the patient and the records wanted, and states the preferred format, such as paper, electronic file, or portal download. Providers may charge a reasonable copying fee under the applicable rules and must respond within a set time, though the exact time limit and fee rules vary. Keeping a personal set of records is useful when changing providers, seeking a second opinion, or checking that a record is complete.

Method. The working method is a written request with a paper trail. First, list the providers and the date ranges wanted. Second, write the request stating format and delivery address, and keep a copy. Third, note the date sent and the date a response is due under the provider's stated process. Fourth, when records arrive, check that the expected visits, results, and medicines are present. Fifth, if something is wrong, write a correction request describing the error and the correct information, and keep both letters.

Do not send record requests with sensitive details through insecure channels when a secure portal or mailed letter is available.

title: Telehealth Privacy Habits
body:
A telehealth visit brings the clinic into the patient's home, and privacy habits for the visit protect both sides. A private room or a quiet corner, headphones, and a check that no one else can hear the conversation are the basics. The visit link should come through the provider's own portal or message system, not through a forwarded link from an unknown sender, and recording a visit needs the agreement of the people on the call and may be governed by local recording rules. After the visit, the usual portal habits apply: sign out on shared devices, and check that visit notes and messages went to the right account.

Method. The working method is a before, during, and after checklist. Before the visit, choose a private space, test audio and video, and close other apps that might show notifications. During the visit, confirm the clinician's identity and the purpose of the visit, and ask before anyone else joins the call. After the visit, sign out on shared devices, review the visit summary for accuracy, and store any instructions where they can be found later. If the connection drops, use the provider's published phone number to reconnect rather than an unfamiliar number from a message.

title: Advance Directives and Record Access
body:
An advance directive is a document in which a person states health care wishes for a time when they cannot speak for themselves, and often names a person to make decisions on their behalf. Related documents include health care powers of attorney and do-not-resuscitate orders, and the names and legal effects of these documents vary by place. For record access, the key point is that the named decision-maker's authority usually begins when the person cannot decide, and providers may need to see the document before sharing records or accepting decisions. Keeping the documents where the named person and the care team can find them is as important as writing them, because a directive locked in an unknown drawer helps no one in an emergency.

Method. The working method is a document chain. First, write or update the directive with the help the local rules require, such as witnesses. Second, give copies to the named decision-maker, the primary clinician, and any hospital that holds the records. Third, store the original where the decision-maker knows to look. Fourth, review the directive after major life changes and after moving to a new state, because forms and rules differ. Fifth, tell family members that a directive exists and who holds it, without needing to share every detail.
